query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA (with density <6 g/cm³), controlled thermal exposure leads to the in-situ nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic compounds from the original metastable solid‐solution state. These newly evolved phases locally modify the chemistry of the alloy surface, promoting the formation of a more protective oxide/passive film, which in turn reduces the corrosion current density and alters high-temperature oxidation kinetics relative to the unaged (baseline) state.
generation.material_initial_state: A non-equilibrium, metastable Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy produced (for example) via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, featuring a solid solution mixed with minor, non-equilibrium intermetallic precursors while having an overall density below 6 g/cm³.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to a controlled thermal aging treatment (or simulated service heat exposure) designed to drive phase evolution towards equilibrium, thereby promoting the nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Thermal exposure under an oxidizing atmosphere at service-relevant high temperatures (e.g., isothermal exposure at a set high temperature for a defined duration) while keeping all other processing parameters constant. The comparison is between this thermally aged/interrogated state and the as-sintered baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The controlled formation and spatial distribution of stable intermetallic compounds that are richer in elements which form protective oxide scales.
generation.mechanism: Differences in intrinsic diffusivities and chemical potentials among the constituent elements trigger phase segregation upon thermal exposure. The growth of stable intermetallic phases locally alters the elemental distribution at the surface, resulting in modified oxides—such as more continuous Ti- or Zn-rich films—that enhance passivation and change the kinetics of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial baseline, the thermally aged alloy will exhibit a shift in corrosion behavior (e.g., a lower corrosion current density and more noble corrosion potential) as well as modified high-temperature oxidation behavior (such as reduced oxidation rate or improved scale adherence). Specific magnitudes are uncertain, but the direction is toward improved passivation and altered oxidation kinetics.
generation.baseline: The as-sintered non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA with a largely homogeneous solid solution and a metastable distribution of intermetallics.
generation.boundary: Alloy design constrained to densities below 6 g/cm³ and alloy compositions where constituent-property differences favor the formation of intermetallic compounds.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in corrosion resistance and oxidation resistance is not specified by current evidence, although the qualitative trend toward improved passivation due to phase evolution is supported.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples. One set is kept in the as-sintered (baseline) non-equilibrium state, while the other is subjected to a controlled thermal aging treatment (e.g., isothermal hold at a service-relevant high temperature in an oxidizing atmosphere for a predetermined duration). Conduct detailed phase identification (e.g., using XRD and TEM) to confirm the formation of stable intermetallics, and perform surface analyses (e.g., XPS) to characterize the nature of the oxide/passive films. Finally, carry out standardized electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., Tafel polarization in a chloride-containing solution) and high-temperature oxidation measurements (mass gain kinetics) on both sample sets.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and uniformity (XPS, SEM-EDS)
Corrosion potential and corrosion current density (electrochemical testing)
Oxidation kinetics (mass gain measurement over time at high temperature)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal aging (intervened) samples do not exhibit a statistically significant shift in phase composition (i.e., no formation of new stable intermetallic phases) and do not show the predicted changes in the surface oxide characteristics—with no corresponding improvement (or systematic change) in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-sintered control—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys (HEAs), which include multiple principal elements, have attracted substantial research attention due to their exceptional mechanical properties, such as high fracture toughness, hardness, fatigue and corrosion resistances, yield strength, ductility and thermal stability,,,. In many applications, HEAs can significantly outperform traditional and super-alloys, especially at low and high temperatures,. Recently, the design of lightweight HEAs (with a density lower than 5 g/cc) has become one of the hottest research topics in metallurgy. In view of the outstanding performance of HEAs, the lightweight HEAs may have superior performance than traditional lightweight materials such as Al, Mg, and Ti alloys, with a large number of potential industry applications. Yet the chemical and compositional design space of HEAs is exceptionally vast, which makes the use of the traditional experimental methods for HEA screening an overwhelming task. Thus, an efficient, accurate strategy is required for the design of lightweight HEAs for specific applications,. The aim of the present work is to investigate the influence of systematic variations in Mg content on the microstructure, mechanical properties, and corrosion behavior of these alloys. By characterizing the resulting intermetallic phases, grain refinement, and passive film formation, this study identified how processing and composition synergistically affect the corrosion resistance and mechanical performance. This work offers new insights into the design of corrosion-resistant, high-strength materials and represents a novel extension of compositionally complex alloy design to Mg-rich systems.
